claim: Domestic pigeons (Columba livia) exhibit stunning variation in foot feathering within a single extant species.
source: In contrast, domestic pigeons (Columba livia) exhibit stunning variation within a single extant species (Shapiro and Domyan, 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement in the text supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Most pigeon breeds have feet covered by scaled epidermis (wild-type).
source: Most breeds have feet covered by scaled epidermis (wild-type), but scales are replaced by small feathers in grouse (gr) mutants, and by larger feather 'muffs' in birds that also carry mutant alleles at the Slipper (Sl) locus (Doncaster, 1912; Wexelsen, 1934; Hollander, 1937; Levi, 1986) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple historical citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Scales are replaced by small feathers in grouse (gr) mutants.
source: Most breeds have feet covered by scaled epidermis (wild-type), but scales are replaced by small feathers in grouse (gr) mutants, and by larger feather 'muffs' in birds that also carry mutant alleles at the Slipper (Sl) locus (Doncaster, 1912; Wexelsen, 1934; Hollander, 1937; Levi, 1986) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple historical citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Scales are replaced by larger feather 'muffs' in birds that also carry mutant alleles at the Slipper (Sl) locus.
source: Most breeds have feet covered by scaled epidermis (wild-type), but scales are replaced by small feathers in grouse (gr) mutants, and by larger feather 'muffs' in birds that also carry mutant alleles at the Slipper (Sl) locus (Doncaster, 1912; Wexelsen, 1934; Hollander, 1937; Levi, 1986) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple historical citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: In muffed breeds, scutellate scales are generally absent or poorly developed on the feathered epidermis covering the tarsometatarsus and toes.
source: In muffed breeds, scutellate scales are generally absent or poorly developed on the feathered epidermis covering the tarsometatarsus and toes, and feathers are surrounded by soft integument.
evidence: This is a direct observational statement about the phenotype of muffed breeds.

claim: Feathers in muffed breeds are surrounded by soft integument.
source: In muffed breeds, scutellate scales are generally absent or poorly developed on the feathered epidermis covering the tarsometatarsus and toes, and feathers are surrounded by soft integument.
evidence: This is a direct observational statement about the phenotype of muffed breeds.

claim: The molecular identities of both gr and Sl are unknown.
source: The molecular identities of both gr and Sl are unknown, and additional loci probably control quantitative variation in the muff phenotype.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge at the time of writing, prior to the study's findings.

claim: Additional loci probably control quantitative variation in the muff phenotype.
source: The molecular identities of both gr and Sl are unknown, and additional loci probably control quantitative variation in the muff phenotype.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the complexity of the phenotype.

claim: Two loci of major effect (LG11 and LG20) control foot feathering in pigeons.
source: Using quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping with 130 F2 offspring genotyped at 3803 polymorphic markers (Broman et al., 2003), we identified two linkage groups (LG11 and LG20) that had significant effects on three different aspects of foot feathering (log10 odds ratio (LOD) > 4.6; Figure 1B–G, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by QTL mapping data presented in the manuscript.

claim: LG11 had the largest effects on the proportion of the tarsometatarsal epidermis that was transformed from scaled to feathered (LOD = 7.69, PVE = 28.4%).
source: LG11 had the largest effects on the proportion of the tarsometatarsal epidermis that was transformed from scaled to feathered (LOD = 7.69, percent variance explained (PVE) = 28.4%) and toe feather number (LOD = 6.72, PVE = 21.3%), and a smaller effect on toe feather length (LOD = 8.51, PVE = 15.8%).
evidence: This claim is supported by QTL mapping data with specific LOD and PVE values.

claim: LG11 had the largest effects on toe feather number (LOD = 6.72, PVE = 21.3%).
source: LG11 had the largest effects on the proportion of the tarsometatarsal epidermis that was transformed from scaled to feathered (LOD = 7.69, percent variance explained (PVE) = 28.4%) and toe feather number (LOD = 6.72, PVE = 21.3%), and a smaller effect on toe feather length (LOD = 8.51, PVE = 15.8%).
evidence: This claim is supported by QTL mapping data with specific LOD and PVE values.

claim: LG11 had a smaller effect on toe feather length (LOD = 8.51, PVE = 15.8%).
source: LG11 had the largest effects on the proportion of the tarsometatarsal epidermis that was transformed from scaled to feathered (LOD = 7.69, percent variance explained (PVE) = 28.4%) and toe feather number (LOD = 6.72, PVE = 21.3%), and a smaller effect on toe feather length (LOD = 8.51, PVE = 15.8%).
evidence: This claim is supported by QTL mapping data with specific LOD and PVE values.

claim: LG20 had the largest effect on toe feather length (LOD = 20.9, PVE = 52.2%).
source: LG20 had the largest effect on toe feather length (LOD = 20.9, PVE = 52.2%), and a smaller effect on toe feather number (LOD = 5.36, PVE = 16.5%).
evidence: This claim is supported by QTL mapping data with specific LOD and PVE values.

claim: LG20 had a smaller effect on toe feather number (LOD = 5.36, PVE = 16.5%).
source: LG20 had the largest effect on toe feather length (LOD = 20.9, PVE = 52.2%), and a smaller effect on toe feather number (LOD = 5.36, PVE = 16.5%).
evidence: This claim is supported by QTL mapping data with specific LOD and PVE values.

claim: Among F2 offspring, digit 3 bore the largest and greatest number of feathers.
source: Among F2 offspring, digit 3 bore the largest and greatest number of feathers (digit 1, 7.04 ± 5.08 feathers; digit 2, 7.64 ± 7.54; digit 3, 15.46 ± 10.43; digit 4, 6.13 ± 5.70).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from F2 offspring.

claim: F1 hybrids from a cross between muffed and scaled breeds displayed intermediate foot feathering, demonstrating a semi-dominant inheritance pattern.
source: F1 hybrids displayed intermediate foot feathering, demonstrating a semi-dominant inheritance pattern.
evidence: This claim is based on observed phenotypes in F1 hybrids from the genetic cross.

claim: Scaled, muffed, and intermediate phenotypes were recovered in the F2 population, confirming that a small number of major-effect loci contribute to this trait.
source: Scaled, muffed, and intermediate phenotypes were recovered in the F2 population, confirming that a small number of major-effect loci contribute to this trait.
evidence: This claim is based on the distribution of phenotypes in the F2 generation.

claim: The peak pFst region on scaffold 79 contained a 44-kb deletion (from 6.719–6.763 Mb) that was homozygous in 10, and heterozygous in 2 of the 15 feather-footed birds.
source: The peak pFst region on scaffold 79 contained a 44-kb deletion (from 6.719–6.763 Mb) that was homozygous in 10, and heterozygous in 2 of the 15 feather-footed birds (Figure 2B,C; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequencing data and genotyping results.

claim: Birds homozygous for the 44-kb deletion showed elevated levels of haplotype homozygosity relative to scaled birds, a signature of positive selection on this region.
source: Birds homozygous for the deletion showed elevated levels of haplotype homozygosity relative to scaled birds, a signature of positive selection on this region (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by extended haplotype homozygosity analysis.

claim: The 44-kb deletion spans an element orthologous to a known human limb enhancer, hs1473.
source: This deletion spans an element orthologous to a known human limb enhancer, hs1473 (Spielmann et al., 2012), which contains active chromatin marks (Cotney et al., 2012) and is bound by the hindlimb-specific transcription factor Pitx1 in the developing mouse hindlimb (Infante et al., 2013) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative genomics and citations to prior studies.

claim: The hs1473 enhancer contains active chromatin marks.
source: This deletion spans an element orthologous to a known human limb enhancer, hs1473 (Spielmann et al., 2012), which contains active chromatin marks (Cotney et al., 2012) and is bound by the hindlimb-specific transcription factor Pitx1 in the developing mouse hindlimb (Infante et al., 2013) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The hs1473 enhancer is bound by the hindlimb-specific transcription factor Pitx1 in the developing mouse hindlimb.
source: This deletion spans an element orthologous to a known human limb enhancer, hs1473 (Spielmann et al., 2012), which contains active chromatin marks (Cotney et al., 2012) and is bound by the hindlimb-specific transcription factor Pitx1 in the developing mouse hindlimb (Infante et al., 2013) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The 44-kb deletion locus was homozygous in 35 of 54 additional feather-footed birds from 21 breeds, but was never homozygous in 96 scale-footed birds from 56 breeds.
source: The locus was homozygous for the deletion in 35 of 54 additional feather-footed birds from 21 breeds, but was never homozygous in 96 scale-footed birds from 56 breeds (Chi-square, p<0.0001; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by genotyping data across multiple breeds with statistical analysis.

claim: Only the muffed birds (more heavily feathered) showed signatures of selection and shared similar haplotypes on scaffold 70.
source: In contrast to the differentiation signal we observed between scale-footed and all feather-footed birds on scaffold 79, only the muffed birds (more heavily feathered) showed signatures of selection and shared similar haplotypes on scaffold 70 (higher pFst signal than the adjacent scaffold 95) (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplements 2C, 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by pFst and haplotype analysis data.

claim: Mutation on scaffold 79 alone is sufficient for the grouse phenotype (gr locus).
source: Thus, both QTL analyses and whole-genome scans show that mutation on scaffold 79 alone is sufficient for the grouse phenotype (gr locus), and point to scaffold 70 as the major-effect locus for longer toe feathers in birds with muffs (Sl locus) (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This claim is based on the integration of QTL mapping and genomic scan results.

claim: Scaffold 70 is the major-effect locus for longer toe feathers in birds with muffs (Sl locus).
source: Thus, both QTL analyses and whole-genome scans show that mutation on scaffold 79 alone is sufficient for the grouse phenotype (gr locus), and point to scaffold 70 as the major-effect locus for longer toe feathers in birds with muffs (Sl locus) (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This claim is based on the integration of QTL mapping and genomic scan results.

claim: The highest pFst peak on scaffold 79 was approximately 200 kb upstream of Pitx1.
source: The highest pFst peak on scaffold 79 – corresponding to the major-effect QTL on LG 11 for the proportion of tarsometatarsal feathering – was approximately 200 kb upstream of Pitx1, a gene that encodes a homeobox-containing transcription factor that is normally expressed in the vertebrate hindlimb but not the forelimb (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic mapping data.

claim: Pitx1 encodes a homeobox-containing transcription factor that is normally expressed in the vertebrate hindlimb but not the forelimb.
source: The highest pFst peak on scaffold 79 – corresponding to the major-effect QTL on LG 11 for the proportion of tarsometatarsal feathering – was approximately 200 kb upstream of Pitx1, a gene that encodes a homeobox-containing transcription factor that is normally expressed in the vertebrate hindlimb but not the forelimb (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Pitx1 function.

claim: The highest pFst peak on scaffold 70 was 40 kb upstream of Tbx5.
source: The highest pFst peak on scaffold 70 – corresponding to the major-effect QTL on LG 20 for toe feather length – was 40 kb upstream of Tbx5, a gene that encodes a T-box transcription factor that is normally expressed in the vertebrate forelimb but not the hindlimb (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic mapping data.

claim: Tbx5 encodes a T-box transcription factor that is normally expressed in the vertebrate forelimb but not the hindlimb.
source: The highest pFst peak on scaffold 70 – corresponding to the major-effect QTL on LG 20 for toe feather length – was 40 kb upstream of Tbx5, a gene that encodes a T-box transcription factor that is normally expressed in the vertebrate forelimb but not the hindlimb (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Tbx5 function.

claim: Pitx1 and Tbx5 encode key transcriptional regulators of forelimb (Tbx5) and hindlimb (Pitx1) identity and development.
source: These regions were especially intriguing because these two genes encode key transcriptional regulators of forelimb (Tbx5) and hindlimb (Pitx1) identity and development (Logan et al., 1998; Logan and Tabin, 1999; Rodriguez-Esteban et al., 1999; Szeto et al., 1999; Takeuchi et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Misexpression of Pitx1 in the embryonic chick forelimb blocks feather development.
source: For example, misexpression of Pitx1 in the embryonic chick forelimb blocks feather development (Logan and Tabin, 1999), while misexpression of Tbx5 in the early hindlimb field of embryonic chickens is sufficient to induce a partial wing-like transformation, including feather formation on the feet (Takeuchi et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Misexpression of Tbx5 in the early hindlimb field of embryonic chickens is sufficient to induce a partial wing-like transformation, including feather formation on the feet.
source: For example, misexpression of Pitx1 in the embryonic chick forelimb blocks feather development (Logan and Tabin, 1999), while misexpression of Tbx5 in the early hindlimb field of embryonic chickens is sufficient to induce a partial wing-like transformation, including feather formation on the feet (Takeuchi et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior experimental work.

claim: In mouse, Pitx1 (but not Tbx5) plays a role in determining limb-type identity.
source: In mouse, Pitx1 (but not Tbx5) plays a role in determining limb-type identity (Szeto et al., 1999; Minguillon et al., 2005; DeLaurier et al., 2006), suggesting that the roles of Tbx5 in limb outgrowth and identity have diversified during amniote evolution (Horton et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in mouse.

claim: No fixed non-synonymous coding changes in Pitx1 or Tbx5 were identified between scale-footed and feather-footed breeds of pigeon.
source: We did not identify any fixed non-synonymous coding changes in Pitx1 or Tbx5 between scale-footed and feather-footed breeds of pigeon.
evidence: This claim is based on genomic sequencing and analysis.

claim: Pitx1 expression was reduced in both muffed breeds (Indian fantail and English trumpeter) compared to racing homer at HH25.
source: Pitx1 expression was reduced in both muffed breeds (expression relative to racing homer: Indian fantail 0.75 ± 0.06, p=0.0007; English trumpeter 0.40 ± 0.05, p=0.0007; n = 6 each) and was more severely reduced in the large-muffed English trumpeter (p=0.002) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR expression data.

claim: Pitx1 expression was more severely reduced in the large-muffed English trumpeter compared to the small-muffed Indian fantail.
source: Pitx1 expression was reduced in both muffed breeds (expression relative to racing homer: Indian fantail 0.75 ± 0.06, p=0.0007; English trumpeter 0.40 ± 0.05, p=0.0007; n = 6 each) and was more severely reduced in the large-muffed English trumpeter (p=0.002) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR expression data with statistical comparison.

claim: Tbx5 was ectopically expressed in the hindlimbs of both muffed breeds (Indian fantail and English trumpeter) at HH25.
source: Conversely, Tbx5, the forelimb-specific transcription factor, was ectopically expressed in the hindlimbs of both muffed breeds (hindlimb expression relative to racing homer forelimb: racing homer 0.001 ± 0.0004; Indian fantail 0.01 ± 0.008, p=0.0007; English trumpeter 0.14 ± 0.05, p=0.0007; n = 6 each), and was higher in the large-muffed English trumpeter (p=0.002) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR expression data.

claim: Tbx5 expression in the hindlimb was higher in the large-muffed English trumpeter compared to the small-muffed Indian fantail.
source: Conversely, Tbx5, the forelimb-specific transcription factor, was ectopically expressed in the hindlimbs of both muffed breeds (hindlimb expression relative to racing homer forelimb: racing homer 0.001 ± 0.0004; Indian fantail 0.01 ± 0.008, p=0.0007; English trumpeter 0.14 ± 0.05, p=0.0007; n = 6 each), and was higher in the large-muffed English trumpeter (p=0.002) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR expression data with statistical comparison.

claim: Forelimb expression of Tbx5 was indistinguishable among the three breeds (racing homer, Indian fantail, English trumpeter).
source: Forelimb expression of Tbx5 was indistinguishable among the three breeds, indicating that upregulation of Tbx5 in feather-footed breeds is restricted to the hindlimb (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR expression data.

claim: Upregulation of Tbx5 in feather-footed breeds is restricted to the hindlimb.
source: Forelimb expression of Tbx5 was indistinguishable among the three breeds, indicating that upregulation of Tbx5 in feather-footed breeds is restricted to the hindlimb (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that forelimb expression is unchanged.

claim: Ectopic hindlimb expression of Tbx5 in muffed embryos was markedly different than its normal forelimb pattern in wild-type pigeons and other vertebrates.
source: Interestingly, ectopic hindlimb expression of Tbx5 in muffed embryos was markedly different than its normal forelimb pattern in wild-type pigeons and other vertebrates (Gibson-Brown et al., 1998a; 1998b; Logan et al., 1998; Tamura et al., 1999; Ruvinsky et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data and citations to prior work.

claim: Tbx5 is typically expressed throughout the mesoderm of the forelimb.
source: Tbx5 is typically expressed throughout the mesoderm of the forelimb, but ectopic Tbx5 expression was largely localized to the mesoderm of the proximal and posterior-dorsal hindlimb of the small-muffed Indian fantail (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about normal Tbx5 expression.

claim: Ectopic Tbx5 expression was largely localized to the mesoderm of the proximal and posterior-dorsal hindlimb of the small-muffed Indian fantail.
source: Tbx5 is typically expressed throughout the mesoderm of the forelimb, but ectopic Tbx5 expression was largely localized to the mesoderm of the proximal and posterior-dorsal hindlimb of the small-muffed Indian fantail (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data.

claim: The domain of ectopic Tbx5 expression was further expanded in the large-muffed English trumpeter compared to the Indian fantail.
source: This domain was further expanded in the large-muffed English trumpeter (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 3C), consistent with the quantitative differences in expression between the two breeds (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data.

claim: The domain of ectopic Tbx5 expression shows a striking correlation with regions of epidermal transformation, as foot feathers are usually longest and most numerous on the posterior digits.
source: This domain shows a striking correlation with regions of epidermal transformation, as foot feathers are usually longest and most numerous on the posterior digits (Darwin, 1868; Levi, 1986) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D–N).
evidence: This claim is based on correlation between expression domain and phenotype, supported by citations.

claim: Pitx1 had a qualitatively similar expression domain in embryos of scale-footed and feather-footed breeds at HH25, despite quantitative expression differences.
source: In contrast, and despite quantitative expression differences among breeds, Pitx1 had a qualitatively similar expression domain in embryos of scale-footed and feather-footed breeds at this stage (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data.

claim: Expression of the feathered-foot allele of Pitx1 was approximately 20% lower than the scaled-foot allele in F1 hybrid embryos.
source: Consistent with expression differences we observed among breeds (Figure 3A,B), expression of the feathered-foot allele of Pitx1 was approximately 20% lower than the scaled-foot allele (expression of feathered-foot relative to scaled-foot allele: 0.807 ± 0.039, p=0.003, n = 6 embryos), and expression of the feathered-foot allele of Tbx5 was nearly 1600% higher than the scaled-foot allele (relative expression of feathered-foot allele: 15.75 ± 4.69, p=0.002, n = 7 embryos) (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by allele-specific expression assay data.

claim: Expression of the feathered-foot allele of Tbx5 was nearly 1600% higher than the scaled-foot allele in F1 hybrid embryos.
source: Consistent with expression differences we observed among breeds (Figure 3A,B), expression of the feathered-foot allele of Pitx1 was approximately 20% lower than the scaled-foot allele (expression of feathered-foot relative to scaled-foot allele: 0.807 ± 0.039, p=0.003, n = 6 embryos), and expression of the feathered-foot allele of Tbx5 was nearly 1600% higher than the scaled-foot allele (relative expression of feathered-foot allele: 15.75 ± 4.69, p=0.002, n = 7 embryos) (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by allele-specific expression assay data.

claim: Expression levels of feathered-foot and scaled-foot alleles of Tbx3 were indistinguishable in F1 hybrid embryos.
source: In contrast, expression levels of feathered-foot and scaled-foot alleles of Tbx3 were indistinguishable (relative expression of feathered-foot allele: 0.99 ± 0.05, p=0.68, n = 7 embryos) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by allele-specific expression assay data.

claim: Cis-acting genetic changes alter expression of feathered-foot alleles of Pitx1 and Tbx5, but not Tbx3, in the embryonic pigeon hindlimb.
source: These results directly show that cis-acting genetic changes alter expression of feathered-foot alleles of Pitx1 and Tbx5, but not Tbx3, in the embryonic pigeon hindlimb.
evidence: This claim is based on the allele-specific expression results.

claim: Two regions of significantly different H3K27ac enrichment in racing homer hindlimbs relative to forelimbs were within the 44-kb genomic region that is deleted in the Indian fantail.
source: Strikingly, two regions of significantly different enrichment in racing homer hindlimbs relative to forelimbs were within the 44-kb genomic region that is deleted in the Indian fantail, and one of these regions (log10 likelihood ratio = 4.93) is adjacent to the hs1473 limb enhancer (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: One region of differential H3K27ac enrichment (log10 likelihood ratio = 4.93) is adjacent to the hs1473 limb enhancer.
source: Strikingly, two regions of significantly different enrichment in racing homer hindlimbs relative to forelimbs were within the 44-kb genomic region that is deleted in the Indian fantail, and one of these regions (log10 likelihood ratio = 4.93) is adjacent to the hs1473 limb enhancer (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: The most significant differentially enriched H3K27ac region in Indian fantail hindlimbs relative to racing homer hindlimbs was directly upstream of Tbx5 (log10 likelihood ratio = 10.3).
source: Furthermore, the most significant differentially enriched region in Indian fantail hindlimbs relative to racing homer hindlimbs was directly upstream of Tbx5 (log10 likelihood ratio = 10.3) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: The overlapping patterns of H3K27ac enrichment in Indian fantail hindlimbs and wild-type forelimbs suggest that ectopic hindlimb expression of Tbx5 could be due to de-repression of forelimb-specific enhancers.
source: The overlapping patterns of enrichment in Indian fantail hindlimbs and wild-type forelimbs suggest that ectopic hindlimb expression of Tbx5 could be due to de-repression of forelimb-specific enhancers.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the ChIP-seq data.

claim: The fibularis longus (FL) tendon inserts on the dorsal rather than ventral surface of the proximal tarsometatarsus in muffed pigeon breeds.
source: We found consistent soft-tissue patterning defects in both feather-footed pigeon breeds: the fibularis longus (FL) tendon inserts on the dorsal rather than ventral surface of the proximal tarsometatarsus, the flexor perforans et perforatus (FPP3) muscle adopts a longitudinal rather than pennate fiber orientation, and a slip of the FPP3 fuses with the FL tendon (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical observations.

claim: The flexor perforans et perforatus (FPP3) muscle adopts a longitudinal rather than pennate fiber orientation in muffed pigeon breeds.
source: We found consistent soft-tissue patterning defects in both feather-footed pigeon breeds: the fibularis longus (FL) tendon inserts on the dorsal rather than ventral surface of the proximal tarsometatarsus, the flexor perforans et perforatus (FPP3) muscle adopts a longitudinal rather than pennate fiber orientation, and a slip of the FPP3 fuses with the FL tendon (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical observations.

claim: A slip of the FPP3 fuses with the FL tendon in muffed pigeon breeds.
source: We found consistent soft-tissue patterning defects in both feather-footed pigeon breeds: the fibularis longus (FL) tendon inserts on the dorsal rather than ventral surface of the proximal tarsometatarsus, the flexor perforans et perforatus (FPP3) muscle adopts a longitudinal rather than pennate fiber orientation, and a slip of the FPP3 fuses with the FL tendon (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical observations.

claim: The fibula was enlarged in feather-footed pigeon breeds.
source: We also found that the fibula, which is normally splint-like and shorter than the tibia in pigeons, was enlarged (Figure 5D,E) and two phalanges of digit 4 were fused in feather-footed breeds (not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical observations and imaging data.

claim: Two phalanges of digit 4 were fused in feather-footed pigeon breeds.
source: We also found that the fibula, which is normally splint-like and shorter than the tibia in pigeons, was enlarged (Figure 5D,E) and two phalanges of digit 4 were fused in feather-footed breeds (not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical observations.

claim: All of the modified structures of ptilopodous pigeons develop in the posterior (lateral in the adult) and dorsal hindlimb, which are the primary sites of ectopic Tbx5 expression.
source: Notably, all of the modified structures of ptilopodous pigeons develop in the posterior (lateral in the adult) and dorsal hindlimb, which are the primary sites of ectopic Tbx5 expression.
evidence: This claim is based on correlation between anatomical changes and expression domain.

claim: Tbx5 was ectopically expressed at HH25 in hindlimb buds of two feather-footed chicken breeds, the Cochin and the silkie.
source: Similar to pigeons, Tbx5 was ectopically expressed at HH25 in hindlimb buds of two feather-footed chicken breeds, the Cochin and the silkie (hindlimb expression relative to white leghorn forelimb: white leghorn 0.005 ± 0.004; Cochin 0.066 ± 0.050, p=0.002; silkie 0.034 ± 0.014, p=0.009; n = 6 white leghorns, 6 Cochins, 4 silkies) (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR expression data in chickens.

claim: Ectopic Tbx5 expression in feathered-foot chicken embryos had a similar domain to that of feathered-foot pigeon embryos at HH25.
source: Ectopic Tbx5 expression in feathered-foot chicken embryos had a similar domain to that of feathered-foot pigeon embryos at HH25 (Figure 3I,J) and, as in pigeons, cis-acting changes contributed to this expression (expression of feathered-foot allele relative to scaled-foot allele in HH25 silkie x white leghorn F1 hybrid hindlimbs: 1.80 ± 0.41, p=2.55 x 10–5, n = 11 hybrid embryos) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data in chickens.

claim: Cis-acting changes contributed to ectopic Tbx5 expression in feathered-foot chickens.
source: Ectopic Tbx5 expression in feathered-foot chicken embryos had a similar domain to that of feathered-foot pigeon embryos at HH25 (Figure 3I,J) and, as in pigeons, cis-acting changes contributed to this expression (expression of feathered-foot allele relative to scaled-foot allele in HH25 silkie x white leghorn F1 hybrid hindlimbs: 1.80 ± 0.41, p=2.55 x 10–5, n = 11 hybrid embryos) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by allele-specific expression assay data in chickens.

claim: Tbx5-related developmental mechanisms may, in part, underlie the evolution of foot feathering in pigeons and chickens, two species that last shared a common ancestor over 80 million years ago.
source: Hence, Tbx5-related developmental mechanisms may, in part, underlie the evolution of foot feathering in two species that last shared a common ancestor over 80 million years ago (Claramunt and Cracraft, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the convergent expression patterns in two species, with a citation for divergence time.

claim: Classical genetic studies implicate at least two loci in heavy foot feathering in chickens.
source: Classical genetic studies implicate at least two loci in heavy foot feathering in chickens (Punnett and Bailey, 1918; Lambert and Knox, 1929; Warren, 1948; Somes, 1992), although the molecular genetic origins of the trait remain unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classical genetic studies.

claim: A chromosome region containing Pitx1 was implicated in foot feathering in silkie chickens.
source: Previously, a chromosome region containing Pitx1 was implicated in foot feathering in silkie chickens (Dorshorst et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: No statistically significant changes in Pitx1 expression were detected between scaled-foot (white leghorn) and feathered-foot (silkie and Cochin) chicken embryos at HH25.
source: However, we did not detect statistically significant changes in Pitx1 expression between scaled-foot (white leghorn) and feathered-foot (silkie and Cochin) chicken embryos at HH25 (expression relative to white leghorn: Cochin 0.92 ± 0.24, p=0.93; silkie 0.71 ± 0.18, p=0.18; n = 6 each) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR expression data in chickens.

claim: Tbx3 was not upregulated in ptilopodous chicken breeds, in contrast to results in feather-footed pigeons.
source: Also in contrast to our results in feather-footed pigeons, Tbx3 was not upregulated in ptilopodous chicken breeds (white leghorn 1 ± 0.17, silkie 0.48 ± 0.18, p=0.004; Cochin 0.86 ± 0.44, p=0.40; silkie vs. Cochin p=0.07; n = 6 samples each) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR expression data in chickens.

claim: Both shared and distinct mechanisms regulate foot feathering among avian species.
source: In all, these results suggest that both shared and distinct mechanisms regulate foot feathering among avian species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of pigeon and chicken data.

claim: Feathered feet in pigeons result from a partial transformation from hindlimb to forelimb identity mediated by cis-regulatory changes in Pitx1 and Tbx5.
source: We found that feathered feet in pigeons result from a partial transformation from hindlimb to forelimb identity mediated by cis-regulatory changes in the genes encoding the hindlimb-specific transcription factor Pitx1 and forelimb-specific transcription factor Tbx5.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Ectopic expression of Tbx5 is associated with foot feathers in chickens.
source: We also found that ectopic expression of Tbx5 is associated with foot feathers in chickens, suggesting similar molecular pathways underlie phenotypic convergence between these two species.
evidence: This claim is supported by expression data in chickens.

claim: Similar molecular pathways underlie phenotypic convergence of foot feathering between pigeons and chickens.
source: We also found that ectopic expression of Tbx5 is associated with foot feathers in chickens, suggesting similar molecular pathways underlie phenotypic convergence between these two species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the convergent expression patterns.

claim: Changes in expression of regional patterning genes can generate localized changes in organ fate and morphology.
source: These results show how changes in expression of regional patterning genes can generate localized changes in organ fate and morphology, and provide viable molecular mechanisms for diversity in hindlimb scale and feather distribution.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The study provides viable molecular mechanisms for diversity in hindlimb scale and feather distribution.
source: These results show how changes in expression of regional patterning genes can generate localized changes in organ fate and morphology, and provide viable molecular mechanisms for diversity in hindlimb scale and feather distribution.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Most birds possess scales on the foot (tarsometatarsus and toes) and feathers elsewhere.
source: Most birds possess scales on the foot (tarsometatarsus and toes) and feathers elsewhere.
evidence: This is a statement of general knowledge about bird anatomy.

claim: Some raptors and boreal birds evolved foot feathers instead of scales ('ptilopody').
source: Some raptors and boreal birds evolved foot feathers instead of scales ('ptilopody'; Danforth, 1919; Lucas and Stettenheim, 1972), but the lack of appendage variation within these species precludes their use as genetic models.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The lack of appendage variation within raptors and boreal birds precludes their use as genetic models.
source: Some raptors and boreal birds evolved foot feathers instead of scales ('ptilopody'; Danforth, 1919; Lucas and Stettenheim, 1972), but the lack of appendage variation within these species precludes their use as genetic models.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of these species for genetic studies.

claim: Paravians (birds and their close non-avian theropod dinosaur relatives) and other dinosaurs evolved diverse feather coverings on their legs and feet that sometimes resemble flight-like feathers.
source: Likewise, paravians (birds and their close non-avian theropod dinosaur relatives) and other dinosaurs evolved diverse feather coverings on their legs and feet that sometimes resemble flight-like feathers (Xu et al., 2003; Hu et al., 2009; Turner et al., 2012; Zheng et al., 2013; Foth et al., 2014; Godefroit et al., 2014), but the absence of living specimens preclude mechanistic molecular studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to paleontological studies.

claim: The absence of living specimens of paravians precludes mechanistic molecular studies.
source: Likewise, paravians (birds and their close non-avian theropod dinosaur relatives) and other dinosaurs evolved diverse feather coverings on their legs and feet that sometimes resemble flight-like feathers (Xu et al., 2003; Hu et al., 2009; Turner et al., 2012; Zheng et al., 2013; Foth et al., 2014; Godefroit et al., 2014), but the absence of living specimens preclude mechanistic molecular studies.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of studying extinct species.

claim: During development in vertebrates, skin appendages form through interactions between the ectoderm-derived epidermis and the mesoderm-derived dermis.
source: During development in vertebrates, skin appendages form through interactions between the ectoderm-derived epidermis and the mesoderm-derived dermis, and signals from the dermis determine epidermal appendage fate (Dhouailly, 2009; Hughes et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Signals from the dermis determine epidermal appendage fate.
source: During development in vertebrates, skin appendages form through interactions between the ectoderm-derived epidermis and the mesoderm-derived dermis, and signals from the dermis determine epidermal appendage fate (Dhouailly, 2009; Hughes et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Previous analyses of mutants and gene misexpression in chickens suggest candidates for feathered feet in the Hedgehog, BMP, Delta-Notch, and Wnt pathways.
source: Previous analyses of mutants and gene misexpression in chickens suggest candidates for feathered feet in the Hedgehog (Harris et al., 2002), BMP (Zou and Niswander, 1996; Harris et al., 2002; 2004), Delta-Notch (Crowe et al., 1998), and Wnt (Chang et al., 2004) pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The study of genetic variation and embryonic development in pigeons reveals a surprisingly different mechanism for feathered feet than previously suggested pathways.
source: Previous analyses of mutants and gene misexpression in chickens suggest candidates for feathered feet in the Hedgehog (Harris et al., 2002), BMP (Zou and Niswander, 1996; Harris et al., 2002; 2004), Delta-Notch (Crowe et al., 1998), and Wnt (Chang et al., 2004) pathways. Our study of genetic variation and embryonic development in pigeons, however, reveals a surprisingly different mechanism with broad implications for limb identity and patterning.
evidence: This is inferred from the contrast between prior work and the current study's findings.

claim: The average number of mapped reads among F2 individuals was 3,397,598, with a mean depth of 6.3x.
source: The average number of mapped reads among F2 individuals was 3,397,598, with a mean depth of 6.3x.
evidence: This is a technical detail about the sequencing data.

claim: Markers showing segregation distortion (Chi-square, p<0.05) were removed from the genetic map.
source: Markers showing segregation distortion (Chi-square, p<0.05) were removed.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about data filtering.

claim: 3803 markers were assembled into linkage groups.
source: 3803 markers were assembled into linkage groups using the parameters (max.rf = 0.15, min.lod = 6).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about genetic map construction.

claim: Significance thresholds of α = 0.05 were calculated with 1000 permutations of each phenotype across all linkage groups.
source: Significance thresholds of α = 0.05 were calculated with 1000 permutations of each phenotype across all linkage groups.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about statistical analysis.

claim: Mutations at Pitx1 and Tbx5 can cause congenital limb deformities in humans, including clubfoot and Liebenberg syndrome (Pitx1), and Holt-Oram syndrome (Tbx5).
source: Mutations at these genes can cause congenital limb deformities in humans, including clubfoot and Liebenberg syndrome (Pitx1; Gurnett et al., 2008; Spielmann et al., 2012), and Holt-Oram syndrome (Tbx5; Basson et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on human genetics.

claim: Haploinsufficiency causes human limb syndromes associated with Pitx1 and Tbx5.
source: Notably, haploinsufficiency causes these human syndromes, and clubfoot is partially penetrant in Pitx1+/- mice (Alvarado et al., 2011), collectively pointing to an exquisite sensitivity of limb morphology to levels of Pitx1 and Tbx5 gene products.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Clubfoot is partially penetrant in Pitx1+/- mice.
source: Notably, haploinsufficiency causes these human syndromes, and clubfoot is partially penetrant in Pitx1+/- mice (Alvarado et al., 2011), collectively pointing to an exquisite sensitivity of limb morphology to levels of Pitx1 and Tbx5 gene products.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Limb morphology is exquisitely sensitive to levels of Pitx1 and Tbx5 gene products.
source: Notably, haploinsufficiency causes these human syndromes, and clubfoot is partially penetrant in Pitx1+/- mice (Alvarado et al., 2011), collectively pointing to an exquisite sensitivity of limb morphology to levels of Pitx1 and Tbx5 gene products.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited evidence of haploinsufficiency effects.

claim: Pitx1 is involved repeatedly in the evolution of adaptive pelvic fin loss in stickleback fish.
source: Pitx1 is also involved repeatedly in the evolution of adaptive pelvic fin loss in stickleback fish (Cresko et al., 2004; Shapiro et al., 2004; 2006; Coyle et al., 2007; Chan et al., 2010; Shikano et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Threespine sticklebacks that are homozygous for a Pitx1 pelvic enhancer deletion have severely reduced or absent pelvises.
source: Threespine sticklebacks that are homozygous for a Pitx1 pelvic enhancer deletion have severely reduced or absent pelvises, but heterozygotes also have smaller pelvises, thereby allowing natural selection to act on fish carrying one mutant allele (Shapiro et al., 2004; Chan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Heterozygotes for a Pitx1 pelvic enhancer deletion in threespine sticklebacks have smaller pelvises, allowing natural selection to act on fish carrying one mutant allele.
source: Threespine sticklebacks that are homozygous for a Pitx1 pelvic enhancer deletion have severely reduced or absent pelvises, but heterozygotes also have smaller pelvises, thereby allowing natural selection to act on fish carrying one mutant allele (Shapiro et al., 2004; Chan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Increased foot feathering was observed in pigeons with just one derived allele of Pitx1 or Tbx5.
source: Similarly, we observed increased foot feathering in pigeons with just one derived allele of Pitx1 or Tbx5 (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the QTL mapping data showing effects of heterozygotes.

claim: Ancient pigeon breeders could have rapidly selected for ptilopodous pigeon lines starting with birds that were heterozygous for mutations at either locus.
source: Ancient pigeon breeders could have rapidly selected for ptilopodous pigeon lines starting with birds that were heterozygous for mutations at either locus, and later generated the extreme muffed phenotype by hybridization.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the history of pigeon breeding.

claim: The extreme muffed phenotype could have been generated by hybridization.
source: Ancient pigeon breeders could have rapidly selected for ptilopodous pigeon lines starting with birds that were heterozygous for mutations at either locus, and later generated the extreme muffed phenotype by hybridization.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the history of pigeon breeding.

claim: Additional, as yet unidentified, mutations contribute to the muff phenotype.
source: In addition to implicating cis- acting mutations in Pitx1 and Tbx5 driving transformation of scales into feathers in domestic pigeon, our results suggest that additional, as yet unidentified, mutations contribute to the muff phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of quantitative differences in expression.

claim: Misregulation of Pitx1 and Tbx5 was more severe in the large-muffed English trumpeter than in the small-muffed Indian fantail.
source: Although all feathered-foot embryos examined in our gene expression experiments contained derived Pitx1 and Tbx5 haplotypes, misregulation of each gene was more severe in the large-muffed English trumpeter than in the small-muffed Indian fantail.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR expression data.

claim: The English trumpeter may contain additional cis-acting mutations at Pitx1 and/or Tbx5, and/or mutations in upstream regulators of these genes.
source: The English trumpeter may therefore contain additional cis-acting mutations at one or both loci, and/or mutations in upstream regulators of Pitx1 and Tbx5.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the expression differences.

claim: There is a quantitative link between transcription factor abundance and skin appendage fate and morphology.
source: Our findings suggest a quantitative link between transcription factor abundance and skin appendage fate and morphology, thereby highlighting foot-feathering in pigeons as a model for studying the regulatory interactions that govern expression of these two important determinants of limb morphology.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between expression levels and phenotype.

claim: Most modern wild birds have a scaled metatarsus and toes.
source: Most modern wild birds have a scaled metatarsus and toes, although some species (e.g., ptarmigan, snowy owl, and golden eagle) have extensive foot feathering.
evidence: This is a statement of general knowledge about bird anatomy.

claim: Some modern wild bird species (e.g., ptarmigan, snowy owl, and golden eagle) have extensive foot feathering.
source: Most modern wild birds have a scaled metatarsus and toes, although some species (e.g., ptarmigan, snowy owl, and golden eagle) have extensive foot feathering.
evidence: This is a statement of general knowledge about bird anatomy.

claim: Recent paleontological evidence suggests that feathers – not scales – might be the ancestral hindlimb skin appendages in birds and some of their close non-avian dinosaur relatives.
source: However, recent paleontological evidence suggests that feathers – not scales – might be the ancestral hindlimb skin appendages in birds and some of their close non-avian dinosaur relatives (Hu et al., 2009; Zheng et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to paleontological studies.

claim: The epidermis of feather-footed modern birds might represent a reversion to the ancestral avialan skin condition.
source: Thus, the epidermis of feather-footed modern birds might actually represent a reversion to the ancestral avialan skin condition.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on paleontological evidence.

claim: The large, asymmetric-vaned, pennaceous metatarsal feathers of basal birds and their non-avian dinosaur relatives have been interpreted as 'hind wings', although they clearly retain hindlimb skeletal identity.
source: In some cases, the large, asymmetric-vaned, pennaceous metatarsal feathers of basal birds and their non-avian dinosaur relatives are so extensive that their hindlimbs have been interpreted as 'hind wings', although they clearly retain hindlimb skeletal identity (Zheng et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Long foot feathers in basal birds and non-avian dinosaurs are directed laterally from the foot and display vane width asymmetries reminiscent of flight feathers.
source: Furthermore, these long foot feathers are directed laterally from the foot, and they display vane width asymmetries reminiscent of flight feathers; we find a similar morphology in muffed pigeons (Figure 5F, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and comparison to pigeon data.

claim: A similar morphology of laterally-directed feathers with vane width asymmetries is found in muffed pigeons.
source: Furthermore, these long foot feathers are directed laterally from the foot, and they display vane width asymmetries reminiscent of flight feathers; we find a similar morphology in muffed pigeons (Figure 5F, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data and images.

claim: Darwin noted of the muffed English trumpeter pigeon, 'Their feet are so heavily feathered, that they almost appear like little wings'.
source: Perhaps not coincidentally, Darwin, 1868 noted of the muffed English trumpeter pigeon, "Their feet are so heavily feathered, that they almost appear like little wings" (p. 155).
evidence: This is a direct quote from Darwin's work.

claim: A relatively small number of genetic changes account for a large proportion of the variation in epidermal appendage morphology and distribution in pigeons and chickens.
source: Building on classical breeding experiments in both pigeons and chickens, we find that a relatively small number of genetic changes account for a large proportion of the variation in epidermal appendage morphology and distribution.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the QTL mapping and genomic data.

claim: Major determinants of dramatic phenotypic variation can be mechanistically simple and therefore potentially evolve rapidly.
source: Thus, major determinants of dramatic phenotypic variation can be mechanistically simple and therefore potentially evolve rapidly.
evidence: This is a general inference based on the study's findings.

claim: Wing-like foot and leg feathers in non-avian dinosaurs might result from developmental constraints on the morphology of large limb feathers, rather than from functional adaptations for flight.
source: This, in turn, suggests that wing-like foot and leg feathers in other species, such as non-avian dinosaurs, might result from developmental constraints on the morphology of large limb feathers, rather than from functional adaptations for flight (Gould and Lewontin, 1979; Foth et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the evolution of dinosaur feathers, supported by citations.

claim: Limb-type identity is not a simple binary choice between two global fates.
source: This suggests that limb-type identity is not a simple binary choice between two global fates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of partial transformations.

claim: Different aspects of fore- and hindlimb morphology could have different dosage- and/or stage-dependent requirements for exposure to identity cues.
source: Therefore, we propose that different aspects of fore- and hindlimb morphology could have different dosage- and/or stage-dependent requirements for exposure to identity cues.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the observed phenotypes.

claim: The hindlimbs of feather-footed pigeons are still readily recognizable as legs despite alterations.
source: These alterations do not represent a complete transformation of limb type, as the hindlimbs of feather-footed pigeons are still readily recognizable as legs.
evidence: This is an observational statement about the phenotype.

claim: Feather-footed pigeons have a radical transformation of the distal hindlimb dermis.
source: For example, feather-footed pigeons have a radical transformation of the distal hindlimb dermis, yet changes to other hindlimb mesoderm derivatives (muscle, skeleton) are subtler and largely restricted to lateral structures in the adult.
evidence: This is an observational statement about the phenotype.

claim: Changes to hindlimb mesoderm derivatives (muscle, skeleton) in feather-footed pigeons are subtler and largely restricted to lateral structures in the adult.
source: For example, feather-footed pigeons have a radical transformation of the distal hindlimb dermis, yet changes to other hindlimb mesoderm derivatives (muscle, skeleton) are subtler and largely restricted to lateral structures in the adult.
evidence: This is an observational statement about the phenotype.

claim: Tbx3 is a target of Tbx5.
source: This could be due to the fact that Tbx3 is a target of Tbx5 (Mori et al., 2006; Postma et al., 2008), and additional experiments confirm that cis-regulatory changes do not drive this expression difference (see below).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cis-regulatory changes do not drive the expression difference in Tbx3 between pigeon breeds.
source: This could be due to the fact that Tbx3 is a target of Tbx5 (Mori et al., 2006; Postma et al., 2008), and additional experiments confirm that cis-regulatory changes do not drive this expression difference (see below).
evidence: This claim is supported by the allele-specific expression data showing no difference.

claim: Tbx4 is a downstream transcriptional target of Pitx1.
source: The hindlimb-specific transcription factor Tbx4 is not contained in the candidate regions defined by our QTL mapping and genome-wide association studies, but this gene is a downstream transcriptional target of Pitx1 (Logan and Tabin, 1999; Takeuchi et al., 1999; Duboc and Logan, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: No significant differences in Tbx4 expression were found among scaled and feathered pigeon breeds at HH25.
source: We therefore compared expression levels of Tbx4 among scaled and feathered breeds at HH25, but found no significant differences at this stage (racing homer 1.00 ± 0.21; Indian fantail 1.00 ± 0.17, p=0.85; English trumpeter 1.05 ± 0.19, p=0.66; n = 6 each) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR expression data.

claim: Experimental manipulation of Pitx1 and Tbx5 expression can result in muscular and skeletal abnormalities in mouse and chicken embryos.
source: In mouse and chicken embryos, experimental manipulation of Pitx1 and Tbx5 expression can result in muscular and skeletal abnormalities.
evidence: This is a general statement based on prior experimental work.

claim: Pitx1 plays a necessary (but not sufficient) role in determining hindlimb-type morphology of the skeleton, muscles, and tendons in chick and mouse.
source: Experiments in both chick and mouse consistently demonstrate that Pitx1 plays a necessary (but not sufficient) role in determining hindlimb-type morphology of the skeleton, muscles, and tendons (Logan and Tabin, 1999; Takeuchi et al., 1999; Minguillon et al., 2005; DeLaurier et al., 2006; Duboc and Logan, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Experimentally induced ectopic expression of Tbx5 in the hindlimbs of chick embryos can induce muscular and skeletal anomalies.
source: Experimentally induced ectopic expression of Tbx5 in the hindlimbs of chick embryos can also induce muscular and skeletal anomalies, although Tbx5 does not directly control limb skeletal patterning or determine forelimb-type morphology in mice (Rodriguez-Esteban et al., 1999; Takeuchi et al., 1999; Minguillon et al., 2005; Hasson et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Tbx5 does not directly control limb skeletal patterning or determine forelimb-type morphology in mice.
source: Experimentally induced ectopic expression of Tbx5 in the hindlimbs of chick embryos can also induce muscular and skeletal anomalies, although Tbx5 does not directly control limb skeletal patterning or determine forelimb-type morphology in mice (Rodriguez-Esteban et al., 1999; Takeuchi et al., 1999; Minguillon et al., 2005; Hasson et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Normal patterning of limb muscles and tendons is dependent on Tbx5 and Tbx4 in mice.
source: However, normal patterning of limb muscles and tendons is dependent on Tbx5 and Tbx4 in mice (Hasson et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Apparent discrepancies between mammalian and avian systems point to subtle differences in limb development in different lineages.
source: These apparent discrepancies between mammalian and avian systems point to subtle differences in limb development in different lineages (Horton et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative data, supported by a citation.

claim: Experimental ectopic expression of Tbx5 in the hindlimbs of chick embryos produces an enlargement of the fibula reminiscent of extreme pigeon phenotypes.
source: However, experimental ectopic expression of Tbx5 in the hindlimbs of chick embryos produces an enlargement of the fibula reminiscent of extreme pigeon phenotypes, and Takeuchi et al., 1999 compared this morphology to a forelimb-like condition (the fibula "makes a joint at its distal end like a normal ulna [the corresponding postaxial zeugopod bone of the forelimb]," p. 810).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior experimental work.
